item.title: Vatukoula mine workers die before receiving full $25,000 compensation, with 63 beneficiaries still awaiting payments
item.description: More than 30 years of waiting for a resolution to the Vatukoula mine workers’ dispute has raised concerns over delays in the justice system, with Livai Boginivalu telling the Joint Parliamentary Special Committee that many workers have died while waiting for the matter to be resolved. Boginivalu raised the issue during the Constitution Amendment Bill’s public consultation at Wailotua Village Hall
item.content:encoded:
More than 30 years of waiting for a resolution to the Vatukoula mine workers’ dispute has raised concerns over delays in the justice system, with Livai Boginivalu telling the Joint Parliamentary Special Committee that many workers have died while waiting for the matter to be resolved.

Boginivalu raised the issue during the Constitution Amendment Bill’s public consultation at Wailotua Village Hall in Wainibuka.

He says he was one of the workers involved in the Vatukoula strike and claims the workers were told they had won their case, but the matter remained unresolved for decades.

Government compensation payments are now progressing for former Vatukoula mine workers and their families following the strike that began on 27th February 1991.

The Government has allocated $9.2 million for the compensation programme, with 298 beneficiaries having received their full entitlement of $25,000 each, totalling $7.485 million.

Permanent Secretary for Employment, Productivity and Workplace Relations Maritino Nemani handed over payments to 13 former mine workers and beneficiaries.

Seven received their cheques during the presentation, while the remaining six are expected to be paid in the new financial year after administrative and entitlement checks are completed.

A further $1.515 million remains to be distributed to 63 beneficiaries, including people awaiting their full entitlement and estates undergoing probate.

Five beneficiaries who had received an initial payment of $10,000 before their deaths are also owed the remaining $15,000 each.

These payments will be released to their estates once probate procedures are completed.

He also calls for the complete removal of immunity provisions in the Constitution, saying the issue affects everyone.

Boginivalu raises the situation involving Apete Naitini and appeals for the law to be reviewed and clarified.

On the selection of the President, he recommends that the person chosen should be between 60 and 70 years old.

He says the President must be strong enough to carry out the responsibilities of the office and travel around Fiji to engage with people.

Boginivalu also proposes that traditional chiefs be selected through the Great Council of Chiefs, with each yavusa given the opportunity to choose its own chief.

He says the people within each yavusa should be heard and their decisions respected, as traditional leaders play an important role in representing their people.

Boginivalu says these issues need to be carefully considered as the proposed constitutional amendments are discussed.

item.title: Indian national files report with Fiji Police and Immigration Department regarding alleged recruitment scam
item.description: Authorities are working to verify allegations of a recruitment scam involving an Indian national who claims he lost more than $17,000 in connection with arrangements for travel to Fiji and was later threatened and confined at a residence in Koronivia. Speaking to fijivillage News, the man revealed that he first travelled to Fiji in November 2024 after paying an agent in India approximately $5,800.
item.content:encoded:
Authorities are working to verify allegations of a recruitment scam involving an Indian national who claims he lost more than $17,000 in connection with arrangements for travel to Fiji and was later threatened and confined at a residence in Koronivia.

Speaking to fijivillage News, the man revealed that he first travelled to Fiji in November 2024 after paying an agent in India approximately $5,800.

He claims he was detained by immigration officials upon arrival and returned to India.

He alleges the return tickets had been deliberately arranged and claims the individuals involved had already collected money from the applicants.

He says he contacted the alleged recruiter in December 2024 to find out why they had been refused entry, but did not recover his money.

The man says he met the recruiter again in Mumbai in February 2025, when he was asked to pay a further $1,100 for another permit application.

He alleges that in February this year, he paid a further $10,000 in Mumbai after being promised that a work permit would be secured for him.

He claims he was subsequently issued an invitation letter for a business visa, which referred to sugarcane and farming businesses and identified him as a recruitment officer.

However, he says he had expected to obtain employment relevant to his experience and did not want to recruit other people from India.

The man says he arrived in Fiji on 14th September this year, and went to a residence in Koronivia after receiving a location from the alleged recruiter, and that he stayed at the residence for approximately 36 days.

He claims he was repeatedly asked to make payments in connection with the employment and travel arrangements , and that he made several payments.

He claims he paid US$1,045 through an account belonging to the recruiter's nephew and transferred approximately FJD$2,100 through the alleged recruiter's M-PAiSA account.

The man claims he received no assistance with food or living expenses during his stay in Koronivia and had to pay for his own meals and transportation.

He alleges that he also experienced circumstances that caused him to fear for his safety.

He claims he was locked inside the house and threatened, and was warned against disclosing information about the individual or his activities.

He alleges that he eventually managed to leave the residence on 19th October.

He also says that his business visa expired on 28th September and that he had been given a further 21 days to stay in the country.

He says he had also purchased his own return ticket, costing approximately FJD$2,500, which he claims he was unable to use as planned.

He says the circumstances have left him without secure accommodation and that he has been living in fear while seeking assistance and protection.

The man says he has reported the matter to the Indian High Commission in Fiji and the Fiji Immigration Department.

He is also calling for a wider investigation into what he alleges is a recruitment scheme involving more than 60 people from India and Bangladesh.

He claims some individuals may have paid between FJD$10,000 and FJD$12,000 for applications and related arrangements to work in Fiji , and wants authorities to establish whether others may have been affected by similar promises.

He is urging the Fiji Immigration Department to investigate the alleged recruitment activities and the consultancy permit portal.

The man says he wants his money returned and hopes authorities will investigate the allegations and prevent others from experiencing a similar situation.

He believes he has lost valuable time, career opportunities and the chance to advance professionally after trusting the promises made to him.

Meanwhile, Police have confirmed they are working with relevant authorities to verify his allegations.

Questions have also been sent to the Fiji Immigration Department.

item.title: New Rakiraki Immigration Office to ease travel burden for Ra residents
item.description: Residents of Rakiraki and the wider Ra Province will no longer have to travel to Nadi or Suva to access immigration services following the opening of the new Rakiraki Immigration Office. Minister for Immigration Viliame Naupoto says the new office will make it easier for people to access essential government services closer to their homes, reducing travel time and costs.
item.content:encoded:
Residents of Rakiraki and the wider Ra Province will no longer have to travel to Nadi or Suva to access immigration services following the opening of the new Rakiraki Immigration Office.

Minister for Immigration Viliame Naupoto says the new office will make it easier for people to access essential government services closer to their homes, reducing travel time and costs.

Speaking during the opening , Naupoto says development is not only about buildings, roads and infrastructure, but also about improving people's lives, creating opportunities and ensuring communities have access to the services they need .

He says the new office will serve people living in Rakiraki and surrounding areas, including Tavua, Vatukoula, Wainibuka, Nakorotubu and Saivou.

Naupoto says the office will provide passport applications and renewals, citizenship services, permits and visa services.

He says the new system became operational on Wednesday, and the first four applicants received their passports today.

The Minister says the opening follows the establishment of the Nakasi Immigration Office, with plans underway to open additional offices in Nabouwalu in Vanua Levu and Sigatoka.

Meanwhile, Naupoto has reminded immigration officers of the importance of maintaining high compliance standards to protect Fiji's borders while treating members of the public with respect and understanding.

He has urged officers to treat every person with courtesy, listen to their concerns and provide clear guidance.

Naupoto says the government's aim is to ensure that people in rural communities can access essential services without having to travel long distances.
